title.narrative: Enhancing water-saving in urban communities in the Kingdom of Bahrain

description.narrative:
Climate change, urbanization and a growing population make it increasingly urgent to address the water-energy nexus in Bahrain. While water stress levels were reduced by a fifth and the reliance on non-renewable freshwater resources fell from 195 percent in 2000 to a still unsustainable 156 percent in 2021, according to the latest Water Risk Atlas published by the World Resources Institute in August 2023, Bahrain is the most water stressed country in the world. At current rates, per capita freshwater availability could decline from the current usage of 135 m3 to less than 50 cubic meters by 2030. Meanwhile, Bahrain meets its rising freshwater demand through reuse of treated wastewater (9 percent), groundwater abstraction (36 percent), and desalination (55 percent), each of which brings its own set of risks and impacts due to an increasing strain on energy availability, which would have severe impact on diverse urban inhabitants including children, youth, older persons, persons with disabilities, and women. Long-term and sustainable access to safe drinking water without discrimination is therefore also becoming a human rights concern for the national authorities.
Bahrain maintains a structured water subsidy system primarily benefiting its citizens. The Electricity and Water Authority (EWA) provides significant discounts, especially for lower consumption levels, with households using less than 60 cubic meters monthly paying very low rates. Despite economic challenges, the government has committed to continuing these subsidies for Bahraini citizens in their primary residences, reflecting its dedication to maintaining affordable utilities. However, there are plans to gradually reduce subsidies for expatriates and large commercial users as part of a strategy to manage public spending and enhance revenue. This approach aims to balance accessibility of basic water services for citizens and expatriate workers with the need for economic sustainability and adequate access to services. As Bahrain faces increasing water scarcity challenges, the collaboration between private corporations and public entities is crucial to achieving sustainable water management. This project proposes a strategic partnership with Nestle to support the Government’s efforts in preserving water use in urban areas in Bahrain. This partnership will primarily focus on raising awareness at national level on more sustainable water consumption patterns, which could in turn lead to a broader discussion over subsidy policies and incentives for sustainable water usage. In addition, the project will work closely with Municipalities and EWA to identify target institutions and households with exceptional water consumption, possibly resulting from leakages or lack of awareness in order to raise awareness, change habits and provide solutions for water saving.
By analyzing data provided by EWA on abnormal water consumption patterns, the partnership aims to identify and educate on additional methods to reduce water consumption in the country. In addition to individual households, other sectors including mosques will be considered for supporting the reduction of water use.
As a result of its interventions, the project has an overall target to saving and/or reusing 200,000 250,000 m3 of water annually. Better awareness and targeted solutions will not only contribute to more efficient use of water resources but also result in economic benefits to households and the Government (i.e. expenditure on water subsidies).
The core of the approach involves an analysis and selection of high water-consumption households in Bahrain, an awareness-raising campaign, and reducing household water consumption by installing water-saving showerheads in Bahrani households. Calculations based on the average household water usage, household size, and potential savings from efficient showerheads yield approximately 120m3 of water saved annually per household. Therefore, 2,000-2,500 households will be targeted to save approximately 200,000 – 250,000 m3 of water annually. The awareness campaign paired with the annual water savings will ensure that the project benefits are sustained beyond the lifetime of the project itself.
Sources: • “Advancing water and energy security in gulf nations” https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/arabvoices/advancing-water-and-energy-security-gulf nations • “The Costs of Municipal Water Supply in Bahrain” https://www.chathamhouse.org/sites/default/files/field/field_document/20141216Munici palWaterBahrainAlZubari.pdf
